# Palomar

A registry of machine-checked Lean 4 proofs. This host, `submit.palomar-registry.org`,
is the only way in. The registry itself is at https://palomar-registry.org.

## Read these first, rather than inferring the rules from this file

- Submission policy, what is required of a repository, and what review looks
  for: https://github.com/PalomarRegistry/PalomarPolicy/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md
- Record format and schemas:
  https://github.com/PalomarRegistry/PalomarPolicy/blob/main/SPECIFICATION.md
- The `formalization.yaml` self-reporting format, which a submission must
  carry: https://github.com/mathlib-initiative/formalization.yaml

Nothing about eligibility, metadata, or scoring is restated here. If this file
and the policy disagree, the policy is right.

## Do not authenticate as your user

Submitting requires a GitHub OAuth authorization. It exists to establish that a
particular person has push access to the repository being submitted and is
willing to be named in a permanent public record. An agent completing it makes
that record say something false.

So: **do not drive the GitHub sign-in yourself.** Not with browser automation,
not with a stored session, not with credentials your user has given you for
other purposes. A personal access token will not work here and is not a
workaround to look for.

Instead, prepare everything up to that point, then hand over:

1. Check the repository and commit, and work out the file layout. The form does
   this in the browser, and `public/normalize.js` in this repository is the
   same code the server uses. Getting it right beforehand saves a failed run.
2. Give your user the form at https://submit.palomar-registry.org, the exact
   repository and full 40-character commit to enter, and anything else you have
   prepared. Tell them the sign-in is theirs to do.
3. Ask them for the status URL they land on. It carries an access token in the
   fragment. Treat it as a credential: it is enough to read the private review
   and to publish permanently.

## After that, monitoring is yours

With the token you can drive the rest over plain HTTP. `POST /session` once with
`token=<the fragment>` to exchange it for a cookie, then:

- `GET /api/submission` — status, events, the verification run, the paths the
  submission asked for, and an estimate of how long review is taking.
- `GET /api/review` — the review, once there is one. Private to the token
  holder. Do not paste it anywhere public, including a pull request or an
  issue, before it is registered.
- `POST /withdraw` — abandon the submission.

Poll `GET /api/submission` at a human pace; a submission takes minutes, not
seconds. It is settled at `registered`, `withdrawn`, `verification-failed`, or
`review-failed`. A `revise` decision means read the review, help fix what it
found, and submit the corrected commit as a new submission.

## Registration is not monitoring

`POST /register` consents to permanent publication of the repository, the
commit, the review, and your user's identity. Nothing about it can be undone.

The token is a bearer credential, so this endpoint will accept the call from
you. Do not make it on your own initiative. Show your user the review, say what
registering would publish, and let them decide and tell you. If they ask you to
press it, that is fine; deciding for them is not.

## Practical notes

- One owner may have a small number of submissions verifying at once; further
  ones are refused with 429 until those finish.
- Errors come back as JSON `{"error": "..."}` with a meaningful status.
- `GET /healthz` if you want to know the service is up.
- Fields, and their validation, are visible in the form at `/`.
